abstract: This OECD working paper estimates the risk of automation for jobs across 21 OECD countries using a task-based approach that improves on earlier occupation-level estimates. Rather than treating all workers within an occupation as equally exposed, the study uses PIAAC survey data to assess individual-level task profiles and automation probabilities. The analysis finds that 14% of jobs across OECD countries face a high risk of automation (probability of automation >70%), substantially lower than earlier estimates by Frey and Osborne (47% for the US). An additional 32% of jobs face significant change from automation (probability between 50-70%), meaning these roles will be substantially restructured but not fully eliminated. When including all automation technologies—encompassing AI alongside robotics and digitalization—the share of jobs at high risk rises to approximately 27%. The paper also documents significant cross-country variation: Korea and Estonia face lower automation risk while Austria, Germany, and Spain face higher risk, reflecting differences in industrial structure and workforce composition.
keyFindings: 14% of jobs across OECD countries are at high risk of automation (>70% probability), significantly lower than earlier occupation-level estimates of 47%.
An additional 32% of jobs face significant restructuring from automation (50-70% probability), meaning roughly half of all OECD jobs will be materially affected.
Cross-country variation is substantial: automation risk ranges from under 10% in some countries to over 20% in others, driven by differences in industrial structure and task composition.
When including all automation technologies (AI, robotics, digitalization), approximately 27% of jobs face high automation risk.
Within-occupation variation is large—workers in the same occupation can face very different automation risks depending on their specific task profiles, education level, and workplace characteristics.
methodology: Task-based approach using PIAAC (Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies) survey data covering 21 OECD countries. Individual-level task profiles are mapped to automation probabilities using the Frey and Osborne (2017) methodology refined at the individual rather than occupation level. The analysis covers approximately 200,000 workers across participating countries.
qualifiers: Estimates rely on expert assessments of automation feasibility from 2013, which may not fully capture recent advances in AI and large language models. The task-based approach improves on occupation-level estimates but still depends on PIAAC survey questions as proxies for actual task content. PIAAC data collection periods vary by country. The analysis estimates technical feasibility of automation, not actual adoption rates, which depend on cost, regulation, and organizational factors. Does not account for new job creation from automation-driven economic growth.
